title: After the dams came down

blocks.text: The Elwha River runs north out of the Olympic Mountains to the Strait of Juan de Fuca, west of Port Angeles. It was one of the richest salmon rivers on the peninsula, with all five kinds of Pacific salmon as well as steelhead and bull trout, and runs that some have estimated at hundreds of thousands of fish a year. The Lower Elwha Klallam people had fished it for thousands of years[^klallam].

In 1910 workers began a dam 8 kilometres from the river's mouth to power the mills of Port Angeles. Washington law already required dams to let fish pass, but the Elwha Dam was built without a fish ladder, and when it was finished in 1913 salmon could go no further. In 1927 a second, taller dam was built further up, at Glines Canyon. For a century salmon could reach only the lowest 8 kilometres of a river more than 70 kilometres long. The runs fell to a small fraction of what they had been. Below the dams, the river's bed and the beaches at its mouth, starved of the sand and gravel trapped in the reservoirs, washed away to bare cobbles.

blocks.caption: Glines Canyon Dam on the Elwha River in March 2012, partway through its removal.

blocks.text: For decades the Klallam, fishery biologists and conservation groups argued for taking the dams down. In 1992 Congress passed a law to restore the river, and after nearly twenty more years of planning, the work began on 17 September 2011. The Elwha Dam was gone by the spring of 2012. Glines Canyon Dam, 64 metres high, was taken down in stages, a few metres at a time, and the last of it was blasted away in August 2014. It was then the largest dam removal anywhere in the world.

The hardest problem was the sediment. Behind the two dams lay about 20 million cubic metres of sand, silt, gravel and boulders, a century of what the river had carried down. Lowering the dams slowly let the river cut into it bit by bit, so that the sediment came down as a long series of pulses instead of a single flood of mud.

blocks.caption: The Elwha from the strait to the mountains, 2010 to 2020: the two dams coming down, the sediment behind them washing out, the beach at the mouth growing and salmon moving upstream. Heights are exaggerated. A model.
blocks.task: Play the decade after removal began

blocks.text: The river went to work fast. Within about five years, roughly two-thirds of the trapped sediment had been carried out of the old reservoirs. Much of it travelled all the way to the sea. The river's mouth, which had been shrinking for decades, grew a new delta and beach of about 60 hectares, the biggest change to the shoreline of the Strait in living memory. Sand and gravel settled on the bed of the lower river, making new gravel bars and side channels. The Geology course describes the same work done slowly over thousands of years[^sediment].

The pulse had costs too. For a few years the river ran thick and grey, and the fine silt smothered salmon eggs in the gravel and filled the city's water intake, which needed a new treatment plant. Hatcheries kept some salmon going through the muddiest years[^hatch].

Salmon did not wait. Within weeks of the Elwha Dam's removal, chinook were swimming past its old site. In the autumn of 2014, weeks after the last of Glines Canyon Dam was gone, biologists found chinook above its old site, where no salmon had swum since the Elwha Dam closed the river a century before, and steelhead, coho and bull trout followed into the upper river and its side streams. Divers counting salmon have watched their numbers grow, unevenly, year after year. Some fish that had been trapped above the dams as landlocked populations, like the kokanee of the reservoirs, began running to sea again.

With the salmon came the ocean subsidy of lesson W1, the nitrogen salmon carry from the sea into streams and forests. Researchers found ocean nitrogen turning up again in the insects, birds and plants of the upper river as the carcasses returned. American dippers, small grey birds that feed underwater on insects and salmon eggs, were found to be in better condition and to stay put more along stretches where salmon had returned[^dipper].

blocks.title: Outside
points: The former Lake Mills, behind Glines Canyon Dam, is now a valley of young alder, willow and cottonwood growing on the old reservoir bed, with the stumps of trees cut before the dam was built still standing among them. A short trail from the Olympic Hot Springs road leads to an overlook of the old dam site.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the Elwha
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why could salmon use only the lowest 8 km of the Elwha after 1913?
choices: The Elwha Dam was built without a way for fish to pass
A waterfall blocked the river there
The water above was too warm
items.why: State law required fish passage, but the dam was built without it.

items.ask: Why were the dams taken down slowly, a few metres at a time?
choices: So the trapped sediment came down in pulses, not all at once
Because the law allowed only a few metres a year
items.why: Lowering them gradually let the river cut into the sediment bit by bit.

items.ask: What happened at the river's mouth after the dams came down?
choices: A new delta and beach of about 60 hectares grew
The mouth was blocked and the river changed course
items.why: Sand and gravel that had been trapped for a century reached the sea at last.

items.ask: When were chinook first found above Glines Canyon again?
choices: In 2014, a century after the river was closed
items.why: Salmon moved up as soon as the way was open.

items.ask: How did returning salmon help birds such as dippers?
choices: Their eggs and young, and the insects fed by carcasses, are food
Salmon stir up the gravel and free the insects in it
Salmon clean the water of silt
items.why: The ocean subsidy of lesson W1 returned to the upper river.

summary: **Two dams cut the Elwha off from the sea for a century.** From 1913 salmon reached only the lowest 8 km.
**They came down between 2011 and 2014.** It was then the largest dam removal in the world.
**About 20 million cubic metres of sediment was released.** Lowering the dams slowly let it come down in pulses.
**The river mouth grew a new delta and beach.** About 60 hectares, after decades of shrinking.
**Salmon moved upstream at once.** Chinook passed Glines Canyon in 2014, a century after the river was closed.
**The ocean subsidy returned.** Insects, birds and plants of the upper river took up salmon nitrogen again.

sediment.title: Why lower rivers starve
sediment.text: A reservoir is a still pool where a river drops nearly everything it carries. The water released below a dam is clear and hungry: it picks up sand and gravel from the bed and banks below and carries them off, with none coming down to replace them. Beaches downstream shrink for the same reason.

dipper.title: The dipper
dipper.text: The American dipper walks into fast streams and along the bottom, gripping stones, to feed on insect larvae. It is one of the few songbirds that dives, and it sings through the winter by rushing water.

klallam.title: The creation site
klallam.text: The Klallam tell of a place on the Elwha where the Creator bathed and blessed the people. A pair of rock formations at the spot were drowned by the reservoir behind Glines Canyon Dam, and emerged again when the water drained.

hatch.title: Hatcheries and the wild
hatch.text: Hatchery fish raised during the muddy years were meant as a bridge. Managers kept fishing closed on the Elwha for years after the removals so that the returning wild fish could build up their numbers.
